entries.title:
I'm a platform engineer with a background in site reliability, security, and infrastructure operations. I build Kubernetes platforms, delivery pipelines, and automation that improve reliability and make developers' day-to-day work easier.

My experience spans Python, Go, Linux, Kubernetes, Terraform, Helm, AWS, and GCP. Earlier roles in SRE, security, and technical support shaped how I approach engineering: plan ahead, make systems easier to troubleshoot, and turn recurring operational headaches into maintainable, automation-focused tooling. I also build open-source projects focused on Kubernetes automation, Helm testing, and developer workflows.

I'm looking to stay hands-on, guide technical direction, and help teams build infrastructure they can confidently operate and evolve.

entries.title: Post
paragraphs:
I built a plugin for Helm charts that uses graph-based structural filtering and Python's Hypothesis testing framework to explore input configuration spaces (values.yaml) efficiently, to find the bugs you never thought to test for:

https://lnkd.in/ektqstTY

Most Helm testing validates static configurations and doesn’t exercise the full space of configurable paths or combinations of values.

That leaves many classes of bugs among structural complexities, unaddressed before release:

- One value change can have downstream effects across multiple rendered resources.
- Individually valid settings can fail when combined.
- configurable fields exist only in templates and aren’t documented in values.yaml.
- values paths are effectively dead and never change rendered output.
- Different values within the same type constraints can still produce structurally different behavior.

And all of these cases could pass a static 'helm lint'.

hypothesis-helm attempts to expand automated testing toward the full configuration surface of a chart while filtering redundant cases prior to execution.

The pipeline is roughly:

coalesce values -> pre-filter -> sort -> post-filter -> test -> validate

The tested and rendered manifests that pass hypothesis testing can then be passed through  kubesec or any other tool you already have.

I’ve tried my hand at benchmarking the approach against synthetic charts with varying structures and error distributions, which you can see in the studies/-directory.

I’ve also tested it against public data, including Bitnami. See the report the tool generates for yourself:

https://lnkd.in/eqZRNAqJ

This example includes a lot of diagrams that give us a sense of input value sensitivity in the rendered space, as well as charts' structures.
GitHub - astrivant/hypothesis-helm: Hypothesis testing plugin for Helm

entries.title: Post
paragraphs:
What if a microservice could change how it works, not just how many replicas it runs?

I've been working on Polyad, a Kubernetes operator and Python SDK exploring a different approach to fault-tolerant microservices: applications that participate in their own adaptation as demand, dependencies, and available resources change.

The idea is to give developers a way to write microservices and pipelines by defining both the capabilities and its permitted responses to pressure. I'm hoping this opens the door to strategies of running production near or at-scale, while remaining adaptive and responsive to sudden impulses of traffic.

For example, a service might use high-throughput batch workers when resources are available, switch to a lower-memory implementation when constrained, or share compatible work with an authorized peer. Those transitions need to account for readiness, backpressure, and draining work already accepted in a safe manner.

Polyad coordinates this at two levels:

Within a service: SDK strategies support changes to concurrency, worker profiles, admission, and peer connections.

Across the application: Graphs and nested "PolyGraphs" describe workloads and their relationships, allowing coordinated changes to topology, routing, and capacity within administrator-defined constraints.

This complements infrastructure scaling. KEDA can add replicas; optional VPA integration lets application code understand configured resource bounds and observe and react to current Linux cgroup allocations. 

The application can then adjust how it uses that capacity.

There's a graph-theory component, too: Cheeger bounds help constrain structural bottlenecks. But a well-connected graph is not an SLA guarantee. We also need to measure whether work completes on time, delivers the required capability, and meets the agreed quality level. A service that remains reachable while producing unacceptable results hasn't necessarily remained useful.

I'm exploring these interactions through local, process-based studies before spinning up cloud-based validation: comparing fixed and adaptive systems under controlled load, resource changes, and disruptions, with plots of latency, backlog, service-level attainment (SLA) that's computable at runtime, and adaptation behavior.

The intent is to make adaptation an explicit, testable part of the application contract and engineering process, not just a cascade of infrastructure reactions and PagerDuty pings after something fails.

Code and architecture (WIP):

https://lnkd.in/edjues52

Python SDK:

https://lnkd.in/ep4n-NpJ

Worker adaptation study, with graphs:

https://lnkd.in/enpeacGx

Service composition adaptation study, with graphs:

https://lnkd.in/ew2XgdAX

GitHub - astrivant/polyad: Kubernetes operator and Python SDK for adaptive microservices. Compose graphs across clusters, enforce Cheeger bounds, and adapt topology, traffic and capacity to application demand.

paragraphs: Platform Engineer | SRE | SMB Owner | Building reliable cloud infrastructure and better developer experiences | Kubernetes, Python & Go
Nice way to test and benchmark code going forward:)

Last night I had an idea: what if we had a flame graph that showed not just CPU time, but CPU time specifically spent doing memory copies — and the actual bytes of memory moved.

Today it’s real.

Left side: conventional S3 over TCP.

Right side: S3 RDMA with OSD-direct parallel I/O (ofi-rma token with ofi;verbs transport), plus a new trick where the caller passes an iovec straight to BlueStore so we eliminate the memcpy from bufferlist into the arena.

Results for the same 3.24 GB KV cache load:

Ceph host: 82.8% less CPU time spent in memory copies
GPU host: 92.1% less CPU time spent in memory copies

Ceph went from moving 9.76 GB of memory to move 3.24 GB of useful data… down to 0.16 GB.

When the OSDs write directly into the client window, both ends of the path stop copying the same bytes over and over. The profiler makes the difference impossible to ignore.

We get there by shortening the way.

#ceph #kvcache #s3 #libfabrics

paragraphs: Platform Engineer | SRE | SMB Owner | Building reliable cloud infrastructure and better developer experiences | Kubernetes, Python & Go

Finally, “works on my machine” can come with a proof. 

Writing Kubernetes operators has taught me that the happy path is easy; retries, races, and partial failures are where the assumptions get interesting. 

Love seeing those assumptions made explicit before production gets creative.

Over the last couple of months I have been steadly increasing my work with formal methods whenever I prepare bugfixes or patches for the Linux kernel.

Whenever it makes sense I will have agents build LKMM, CMBC, and TLA+ models run them on very beefy machines.

This has been a game changer for me. Before the rise of LLMs using formal methods was just out of reach given the time constraints of our industry.

I find it very empowering to be able to properly model reference count, rcu, or locking changes to the point where I can consistenly break things and catch really gnarly design issues before anything ever makes it into the upstream kernel.

See https://lnkd.in/dZD2iywy which is the repo where I keep a bunch of this work.Its not very pretty but thats not the job of this excercise. The idea is to get more formal methods into regular development.

As CTO of Amutable I want to ensure that verifiability doesn't just cover the architecture of our system but extends to everything that we do.
GitHub - brauner/linux-formal: TLA+ models of Linux kernel protocolsGitHub - brauner/linux-formal: TLA+ models of Linux kernel protocols

entries.title: Emma Doyle reposted this
paragraphs: AWS Certified Solution Architect | Sr. DevOps Engineer | Ex-Amazonian | DevOps, AWS Cloud & System Design | Infrastructure Automation | Mentor

🧹 Kubernetes 1.37 quietly introduced something DevOps teams are going to love. 

In large Kubernetes clusters, it’s common for users to create PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs), use them with Pods, and later delete those Pods without cleaning up the storage.

And Kubernetes doesn't automatically delete the PVC when its associated Pod is removed — intentionally, to protect against accidental data loss.

Over time, these unused PVCs can accumulate, consuming storage capacity and increasing cloud costs.

So the question for storage and DevOps teams becomes:

Which PVCs in the cluster are no longer being used by any Pod?

Kubernetes 1.37 introduces the "PersistentVolumeClaimUnusedSinceTime" feature to make this information available directly through the PVC status.

Once enabled, the PVC Protection Controller adds an "Unused" condition to the PVC:

✅ "Unused=False" → A running or pending Pod references the PVC
✅ "Unused=True" → No non-terminal Pod references the PVC

This makes it much easier to identify potentially orphaned storage and build cleanup automation around questions like:

👉 “Which PVCs have been unused for 30+ days?”

A small addition to Kubernetes, but a useful improvement for storage management, cloud cost control, and cluster operations.

Reference : https://lnkd.in/gvYfRSUQ

#Kubernetes #K8s #AWS #DevOps #Cloud

entries.title: Given: Julian Picone
paragraphs: February 24, 2024, Emma reported to Julian directly

I had the privilege of working for Julian as the Director of Engineering while I was a DevOps engineer at SBE Vision for over a year and a half. Julian showed endless support for scalability and stability in the DevOps ecosystem of projects and he was always open to hearing about ideas for improvements to the product and codebase. He was also probably the best manager I've ever had and showed support through some of the most difficult times in my life, even when they weren't related to the work. I will miss working for Julian and I highly recommend Julian in any role he pursues in the future.
Engineering Manager - DevOps at SBE Vision
February 24, 2024, Emma reported to Joseph directly

I had the privilege of working with Joseph as my DevOps Lead for over a year and a half while I was a DevOps engineer at SBE Vision. Joseph always kept a level head and had business goals and customers in mind while we worked on some of the most complex and capable Kubernetes orchestration and pipeline architectures I've yet encountered in my career. His project management skills were paramount to the team's success in such a small but incredibly fast-paced startup. We accomplished a lot with his leadership despite being a small team with such a broad suite of responsibilities. I will definitely miss working with Joseph and I'd recommend him for any role he pursues in his career.
